doc.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998

title: Hearing Dizzy Gillespie, live bebop in Los Angeles, and rejoining Columbia
summary: He heard Gillespie in 1938, saw Gillespie and Parker at Billy Berg's in 1946, then rejoined Columbia under Wallerstein.

bands.name: Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker Quintet

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Did you personally have — I don’t want to say a problem — how did you adjust in your thinking and listening to the bop movement?

Oh that was a kind of an interesting thing because I was already aware of what was beginning to happen before the war. You see I got drafted straight off the campus, I was inducted about two or three months after I graduated from Yale. The first inkling was in the form of Dizzy Gillespie’s playing. And I first heard Dizzy in I guess it was 1938 because I remember discussing it with Marshall Stearns. His records came out and there were solos of Dizzy’s on various releases, including of course the Cab Calloway Orchestra, and when I got to meet Dizzy it was with Marshall. And I remember Marshall talking to Dizzy. This was in his apartment actually after hours, after a performance in New Haven. And Marshall said, “You know Dizzy on this record you made” — I wish I could remember which one it is — “well you play this figure [scats] what’s the idea behind it?” Dizzy laughed and said, “Oh I thought it was commercial.” Well that broke us up, that Dizzy was probably kidding but at the same time Dizzy was very conscious of the fact that he was doing something different and this was attracting attention to himself. Now I know that this had to be as early as 1938 or ‘39 because Marshall got his Ph.D. and I drove out to California to take his car to Los Angeles and put it on a boat so that he could take it to the University of Hawaii, his first posting with a professorship. And so this had to happen before that trip. And that’s pretty early on for this kind of thing to begin to really take hold. I don’t think there was — well the word “bop” hadn’t come into the picture yet. But more and more there was exposure of this sort. And then when I went away into the armed forces and only got back to New York for very short periods for a couple of years and then not at all when I was overseas, I would hear about what was happening and there were inklings of it on the V-discs of course. And when I came back I went from landing in Seattle to Los Angeles because my sister had gotten married to someone that we knew just before the war, he was a Colonel in the Air Force who got

discharged relatively early, in fact he got discharged when his squadron was brought back to the United States from Europe in order to fly out immediately to Japan and then they were told when they were ready to go, well we don’t need you out there and those of you who have had enough service can get discharged. And that’s when he married my sister and moved out to Los Angeles, his home. So with the permission of my parents, who were very nice about it when I called up in Seattle and said, “Hi Mom and Pop I’m back, can I go visit Mary,” my sister, “before I come home?” Because they always said if you want to do that you’re entitled to it, you’re allowed a stopover. The reason I got into all this is that when I arrived, Ross Russell, who had a record shop in a small record label that he’d just started, Dial Records, was someone I’d met before I went overseas, and he’d been corresponding with me and told me about the growth of the bop movement around Los Angeles. And when I called up Ross he said, “Hey you came just in time, Gillespie and Parker have a quintet at Billy Berg’s and we’ll go tomorrow night if you’re free.” I said fine. That was my first exposure to live bebop. And it was very lively, believe me, and it was very unusual because the records that I had heard were not really indicative of the music that I heard that night. So I heard the group maybe once more before I went back to New York and that was my real introduction to bop. It was puzzling but it wasn’t that far out as we know now by listening to the records. For some people it was very violently different. Now when I got back home, I called up Ted Wallerstein, the president of Columbia Records, I never called him Ted, he was Mr. Wallerstein, believe me, a wonderful man but rather austere and he was the man who hired me to do that great series of the Hot Jazz Classics reissues. He said, “George, you know you’re being drafted and you have to be in the Army for year” that was the way it went before the war reached the United States. “At the end of the year if your father allows you do so, instead of going into the family business because he knew my father wanted me to do that, I wanted you to know you’d be welcome, we’d like to have you back.” And I said, “Gee thank you sir.” And so four and a half years later I called him up and said, “Well I’m back and if that offer still holds, I’d love to come work for Columbia Records full time.” And he said to me, “Well did you ask your father, what did he say?” I said, “Oh my father said, ‘George you deserve to have a little fun. If you want to do that go right ahead and when you want to get serious with your life, come in to the family business,’” which I did 25 years later when my dad was quite old and wanted me to come in, and I felt like it because I got kind of fed up with the changes in the record business. Not things like bop and all, but the commercial aspect and the fact that accountants and lawyers took over the running of the companies, and people weren’t very interested in music anymore.
